title: Well awake (296–305)
hookLine: the disciples of Gotama are always well awake, day and night their minds on the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha
carry: a mind that keeps returning home

lines: THE FIRST THING IN THE MORNING.
cards: What's the last thing on your mind before you fall asleep? For a lot of people it's the glow of a screen, a worry about tomorrow, or a replay of something awkward said at lunch.
And the first thing in the morning is often the same worry, picking up where it left off. Whatever the mind rests on at the edges of the day tends to color everything in between.
Today's verses describe people whose minds rest somewhere else, day and night, and they use the word that gives the Buddha his name.

teach.b: Verse two hundred ninety-six, in Max Müller's English: "The disciples of Gotama (Buddha) are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on Buddha." Gotama is the Buddha's family name.

teach.h: BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA, DAY AND NIGHT.
teach.b: The words for well awake come from the same root as the word Buddha itself, budh, to wake up. A buddha is one who has woken, and his students, the verse says, are well awake too.
Then the verse repeats like a chant, six times over. Well awake, their thoughts set on the Buddha. Then on the dhamma, the teaching.
Then on the sangha, the community. Müller, writing in 1881, translated sangha as the church, which tells you something about his own world.
Those first three are the three jewels from camp three, the three things Buddhists go to for refuge.
The next three verses keep going: their thoughts set on the body, then delighting in harmlessness, then delighting in meditation. So well awake doesn't mean never sleeping.
It means the mind has a home to return to. The rest of the chapter gathers other sayings. Leaving the world is hard, the text says, and living in a household is hard too; both have their pains.
Good people shine from far away like the Himalayas, while the bad go unseen, like arrows shot at night.
And the chapter ends with the one who sits alone, sleeps alone, walks alone, and finds joy in it, as if living in a forest.
In many Buddhist homes, the three jewels are recalled at the end of the day, before sleep: a short homage, a bow, a moment of remembering.

how: Many Buddhists recall the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha at the start and end of the day, often with a bow and a short Pali homage before a home shrine; Theravada teachers call this recollection of the three jewels.

o: a monk who has reached full awakening
someone who never needs to sleep at night
a mind that keeps turning to the three jewels

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.

s: it means the mind has a home to return to, day and night.
the word for 'well awake' shares a root with 'Buddha'
both come from budh, to wake up.
the verse about the three jewels appears only once
it repeats like a chant: Buddha, dhamma, sangha, then body, harmlessness and meditation.

games.q: it's bedtime and your mind is replaying an awkward moment from lunch. what do today's verses offer?
o: turn the mind toward the three jewels for a few breaths.
stay up until you're too tired to think.
games.why: the verses describe minds set, day and night, on the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha: a home to return to.

practice: Let the body settle as if it were bedtime, and let three things pass slowly through your mind, one with each breath: the Buddha, someone who woke up; the dhamma, the teaching and the way things are; the sangha, all the people, past and present, who have walked this path.
If you're simply learning, just hold the three names, the way you'd hold three stones in your hand. Then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Well awake. From budh, to wake, the same root as Buddha: a mind that keeps returning home, day and night.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit buddha: one who has woken up, from the root budh.

carryVoice: Your line: a mind that keeps returning home. Buddha, dhamma, sangha, day and night. Rest well.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.q: The disciples of Gotama (Buddha) are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on Buddha.
